content:
You are an expert scheduling formalizer.

Translate each natural-language async planning problem into a JSON scheduling
specification for a CP-SAT solver.

Rules:
1. Each numbered step in the problem becomes exactly one action.
2. Use action="task" for every action.
3. Use the exact ids step1, step2, ..., stepN based on the step numbers in the
   problem text.
4. Use item values identical to the action ids: step1, step2, ..., stepN.
5. Duration must be the integer number of seconds for that step.
6. Add a dependency only when the problem states that one step must happen
   before another. Do not add extra dependencies.
7. Do not add stations, robots, or resources.
8. Output only valid JSON in this exact shape:
{
  "actions": [
    {"id": "step1", "action": "task", "item": "step1", "duration": 120},
    {"id": "step2", "action": "task", "item": "step2", "duration": 300}
  ],
  "dependencies": [
    {"before": "step1", "after": "step2"}
  ]
}
9. Before finishing, verify that:
   - every step from 1..N appears exactly once in actions
   - every dependency endpoint is an existing action id
   - durations are integer seconds
   - there are no duplicate actions

Translate this planning problem into a CP-SAT scheduling JSON spec.

Problem:
To identify hickory trees, here are the steps needed.
Step 1. Purchase a regional tree identification field guide (20 minutes)
Step 2. Locate a diverse deciduous forest plot (1 hour)
Step 3. Check for the presence of large woody husks on the ground (15 minutes)
Step 4. Note the thickness of the nut shell (5 minutes)
Step 5. Observe the overall height of the specimen (10 minutes)
Step 6. Look for shaggy, peeling bark plates (10 minutes)
Step 7. Identify the leaf arrangement as alternate (5 minutes)
Step 8. Count the number of leaflets per leaf stalk (5 minutes)
Step 9. Check for the presence of a large terminal bud (5 minutes)
Step 10. Smell a crushed leaf for a spicy aroma (2 minutes)
Step 11. Examine the twig for a heart-shaped leaf scar (10 minutes)
Step 12. Verify the leaf is pinnately compound (10 minutes)
Step 13. Look for catkins hanging from the branches (15 minutes)
Step 14. Taste the nut meat for sweetness or bitterness (2 minutes)
Step 15. Gather fallen nuts for closer inspection (20 minutes)
Step 16. Measure the length of the terminal leaflet (5 minutes)
Step 17. Compare sample features against guide illustrations (30 minutes)
Step 18. Check if the leaf rachis is hairy or smooth (5 minutes)
Step 19. Pack a backpack with a magnifying glass and camera (15 minutes)
Step 20. Photograph the tree's silhouette (10 minutes)
Step 21. Consult a local botanical map (30 minutes)
Step 22. Rub the bark to check for hardness (5 minutes)
Step 23. Check for deep furrows in the trunk (10 minutes)
Step 24. Look for "Y" shaped branching patterns (10 minutes)
Step 25. Determine if the nut is four-ribbed (5 minutes)
Step 26. Log the GPS coordinates of the tree (5 minutes)
Step 27. Search the forest floor for debris (30 minutes)
Step 28. Check for signs of squirrel activity near the base (15 minutes)
Step 29. Drive to the trailhead (45 minutes)
Step 30. Collect a leaf sample from a low-hanging branch (10 minutes)
Step 31. Record the elevation of the site (5 minutes)
Step 32. Peel a small piece of loose bark (2 minutes)
Step 33. Zoom in on the bud scales with a lens (5 minutes)
Step 34. Check the weather forecast for the hike (10 minutes)
Step 35. Compare the leaf margin serrations (15 minutes)
Step 36. Inspect the area for sapling growth (20 minutes)
Step 37. Scan the canopy for nut clusters (15 minutes)
Step 38. Use binoculars to see upper branch structure (20 minutes)
Step 39. Measure the diameter at breast height (10 minutes)
Step 40. Look for shield-shaped bundle scars (10 minutes)
Step 41. Estimate the spread of the tree crown (15 minutes)
Step 42. Note the color of the inner bark (5 minutes)
Step 43. Walk to a clearing for a better view (15 minutes)
Step 44. Clean the camera lens (5 minutes)
Step 45. Search for old fruit husks from previous years (25 minutes)
Step 46. Check the soil moisture levels (10 minutes)
Step 47. Observe the branching angle of the limbs (10 minutes)
Step 48. Note the presence of any galls on the leaves (5 minutes)
Step 49. Walk around the entire circumference of the tree (10 minutes)
Step 50. Take a bark rubbing with paper and crayon (15 minutes)
Step 51. Fill out an identification worksheet (20 minutes)
Step 52. Cross-reference the findings with an online database (30 minutes)
Step 53. Check for a piths in a cross-section of a twig (15 minutes)
Step 54. Tag the tree with a temporary ribbon (5 minutes)
Step 55. Record the color of the autumn foliage (10 minutes)
Step 56. Put on sturdy hiking boots (10 minutes)
Step 57. Look for diamond-shaped patterns in the bark (10 minutes)
Step 58. Download a tree ID mobile app (5 minutes)
Step 59. Check for winged sutures on the nut husk (10 minutes)
Step 60. Check for the presence of lenticels on the twigs (10 minutes)
Step 61. Check for local companion plants like oaks (20 minutes)
Step 62. Take a photo of the bark texture (5 minutes)
Step 63. Determine the tree's proximity to a water source (15 minutes)
Step 64. Look for epicormic branching on the trunk (10 minutes)
Step 65. Examine the underside of the leaf for pubescence (10 minutes)
Step 66. Locate a mature specimen for comparison (40 minutes)
Step 67. Calibrate the handheld GPS unit (10 minutes)
Step 68. Measure the length of the petiole (5 minutes)
Step 69. Look for signs of hickory bark beetles (15 minutes)
Step 70. Record the tree's health and vigor (10 minutes)
